What can I not miss in Prague?
There are activities a-plenty here, but the non negotiables are strolling through Prague’s beautiful Old Town, spending a sunny day in the scenic Letná Park, and the Malá Strana neighbourhood, where you’ll find Prague Castle. Two tips for first-time visitors: look carefully – even in the most crowded places like Old Town Square, you can find a nice viewpoint, an unexpected cafe, or a historic alley. And
do
get out of the old town to discover other neighbourhoods like Vinohrady and Holešovice – these places are where locals hang out, which often means better (and cheaper) restaurants.
How expensive is Prague?
The city is relatively cheap compared to other European capitals: beer typically costs €5 or less, and a three-course meal averages €30. For better deals, visit local spots in Holešovice, Letná, or Karlín, where beers cost €2.50-3.50 and meals are cheaper than in the city centre. Many restaurants offer weekday lunch specials (look for the ‘polední menu’) with meals under €8. Charles Bridge sits on the Vltava river, and is a spectacle to behold from afar, as well as the view from the bridge being mighty fine in itself. Back in the day, the bridge was the thing that connected Prague’s Old Town to its Prague Castle, so it’s a pretty important part of the city’s history. It’s also featured in a ton of poems and novels, because it’s just that nice. Plus, especially if you go early or late, it’s pretty empty, and it’s the perfect place for a romantic snap for the Insta.

Climb up to Letná Park and get yet another breathtaking perspective over Prague. In the past decade, Prague 7 (first-time visitors, take note: Prague is divided into sections and assigned numbers) has morphed from a sleepy residential neighbourhood into one that’s vibrant and full of cool boutiques and restaurants. Letná Park features a massive kinetic sculpture of a moving metronome; its foundation was once the base of an enormous Stalin monument torn down in 1962. Letná beer garden’s park benches and views of the Old Town across the Vltava are an after-work favourite among locals, dog walkers and international travellers. Note that despite the idyllic picnic setting, you’re not allowed to bring any food or drink from outside into the beer garden.

For the hustle and bustle of Prague, Wenceslas Square is the place. The square has historically held some of the city’s most important historical moments, including major protests. It’s also got that famous statue of St Wenceslas on his horse. Now, not only can you feel its history in the air, but it’s a great spot for shopping, with everything from cafés to clothing. Our top tip is to get the guided walking tour to learn more about the square’s fascinating history.

Feel like an emperor at Prague Castle
Photograph: Shutterstock
Dominated by the Gothic St. Vitus Cathedral, the ninth-century Prague Castle has been a seat of power for Czech emperors, kings and presidents alike. Exploring every corner of these massive fortifications would take an entire trip, so read up in advance and take your pick. Our favourite sights include the tiny houses of Golden Lane, the Romanesque façade of St George’s Basilica, and the manicured landscapes of the South Gardens. Not even to mention Alphonse Mucha’s striking stained-glass windows.

Looking for somewhere to eat around the castle? Try Kuchyň, a Czech restaurant where you can taste the local delicacies, accompanied by great views of the city.

Learn about architectural history at CAMP
Photograph: Shutterstock
Everyone knows about Prague’s main art galleries and museums, but few seem to mention CAMP, the
Centre for Architecture and Metropolitan Planning
. Housed in a striking Brutalist building by Karel Prager, CAMP is a vibrant hub dedicated to the city’s architectural landscape. Here, you’ll find seasonal exhibitions (with English descriptions), such as the current showcase on Prague’s mobility in 2050, alongside lectures, film screenings, and workshops for all ages.
🤫 Insider tip:
I love the cosy café at CAMP with a sunny terrace and very reasonable prices (cappuccino is just 75Kč). There’s also a study room and a small co-working area if you want to bring your laptop along.

Photograph: Shutterstock
Café Louvre
is one of Prague’s historical cafes. Its famous regulars included Franz Kafka, Albert Einstein, and Karel Čapek, the Czech writer who invented the word ‘robot’.
Stepping inside Café Louvre will make you feel like you’ve travelled back in time to the early 1900s. You can visit the café almost any time of the day, whether you’re looking to get some breakfast, lunch, coffee, or cocktails.

PRAGUE
A Romantic 3-Night Escape for Two
Late September · 3 nights · 4 days
Castles at sunrise · candlelit dinners · Vltava sunsets · Pilsner at golden hour
How to use this plan
A relaxed, city-smart itinerary for a couple — roughly Sep 27–30 (arrival evening through departure
morning). It groups sights by neighbourhood so you rarely cross the river twice. Everything is optional:
treat it as a menu, not a checklist. Prices are approximate (Sept 2025–2026, CZK; €1 ≈ CZK 25) —
confirm current rates on official sites before booking.
At a Glance
Weather Days 15–19 °C (60–66 °F), nights 8–11 °C (46–52 °F); crisp and golden, ~6 h of sun,
occasional showers. Sunset ≈ 18:45 (early) → ≈ 18:35 (30 Sep). Pack layers + a light
rain jacket.
Where to stay Old Town / Malá Strana for romance on your doorstep; Vinohrady or Karlín for local
cafés and better value. Book early — late Sept is still busy.
Getting around Most of the plan is walkable. Trams & metro are excellent: 30-min ticket CZK 30,
90-min CZK 40, 24-h CZK 120, 72-h CZK 330 (~€13). Petřín funicular is included.
Validate tickets at first use.
Money Currency: Czech koruna (CZK). Cards are accepted almost everywhere; keep ~CZK
500–1000 cash for small pubs, markets and tips. Tip by rounding up or ~10%.
Note 28 Sep is Czech Statehood Day (St. Wenceslas Day), a public holiday — many
museums offer free entry or run special hours; check ahead.

DAY 4 · Departure One last view before you go
09:00 If your flight/train leaves after midday, climb Vyšehrad — the old fortress on the hill with
sweeping river views, a peaceful cemetery of Czech greats, and almost no tourists.

Tip: Most hotels hold luggage after checkout — leave your bags, take a final walk, and grab lunch
before heading to the airport.
Romantic Highlights — Don't Miss
The couple's shortlist
Sunset at Letná Park with a beer — the postcard view over the red rooftops. • Vltava sunset river cruise
— castle and bridge lights switching on over the water. • Charles Bridge at night — nearly empty,
statues lit, absolute magic for two. • Petřín lookout tower at golden hour — 360° panorama without the
daytime queues. • A beer spa for two — the most Prague of indulgences (and a great photo story). •
Wallenstein Garden peacocks & Baroque loggia — a free hidden gem five minutes from the crowds. •
Classical concert in a gilded hall — Smetana's 'Vltava' played where it was composed. • Candlelit Czech
dinner — duck, dumplings and red wine in a vaulted Old Town cellar.
Eat & Drink Like a Local
Must-try dishes Svíčková na smetaně (sirloin in cream sauce), beef goulash with dumplings, roast
duck with red cabbage, smažený sýr (fried cheese), and sweet trdelník from a
street stall.
Beer culture Pilsner Urquell on tap everywhere; try local microbreweries (Lokál, U Fleků, or craft
bars in Karlín/Holešovice). Beer ≈ CZK 45–120 depending on the neighbourhood.
Where locals go Holešovice, Letná, Karlín and Vinohrady — better and cheaper than the tourist
core. Look for 'polední menu' lunch deals (under CZK 200) at decent restaurants.
Seasonal note Late September is autumn-harvest season: game dishes and burčák (young wine)
appear on menus — try it at a wine bar while it lasts.

Practical Tips & Logistics
• Book ahead: Prague Castle tickets, dinner cruises, beer spas, classical concerts and any Michelin tables —
2–5 days out online (GetYourGuide, official sites).
• Tickets & validation: transport tickets (PID/DPP) must be stamped on first use — buy at machines,
newsagents or the PID app; fines for unvalidated tickets are steep.
• Airport transfer: bus 119 → metro A, or Airport Express bus AE to the main station; ~CZK 100. Ride-hailing
to the centre ≈ CZK 600–800; agree taxi fares in advance.
• Language: English is widely spoken in tourist areas; a smile and 'Dobrý den' (hello) / 'Děkuji' (thank you) go
a long way.
• Safety & etiquette: Prague is safe; watch for pickpockets on crowded bridges and trams. No drones at the
castle. Tap water is safe to drink.
• Practicalities: EU 230 V plug type C/E; emergency number 112; mobile roaming within EU is usually free.

DAY 4 · Departure One last view before you go
09:00 If your flight/train leaves after midday, climb Vyšehrad — the old fortress on the hill with

and pick up souvenirs on Pařížská or in the Havelské tržiště market.
Optional Day-trip note: with more time, Kutná Hora (1 h train; the famous Sedlec Ossuary bone chapel),
Karlštejn Castle (40 min), or Český Krumlov (2.5–3 h each way — better as its own trip).
Tip: Most hotels hold luggage after checkout — leave your bags, take a final walk, and grab lunch
before heading to the airport.

The couple's shortlist
Sunset at Letná Park with a beer — the postcard view over the red rooftops. • Vltava sunset river cruise

Wallenstein Garden peacocks & Baroque loggia — a free hidden gem five minutes from the crowds. •

castle. Tap water is safe to drink.
